unlabelled.title: My Year On A Factory Floor Assembly Line

passages.text: When I was 19, I spent a year assembling electrical relays on a factory floor for $10/hr.
claims: The author spent a year assembling electrical relays on a factory floor at age 19 and earned $10 per hour.

passages.text: I was pretty excited to get the job.
claims: The author was excited to get the factory job.

passages.text: I’d been applying to much worse - I remember looking at at a craigslist ad for a sewage worker, which included a warning that it might be pretty gross.
claims: Before getting the factory job, the author applied for other jobs, including a sewage-worker job advertised on Craigslist with a warning that it could be unpleasant.

passages.text: I applied for that too.
claims: The author applied for a sewage-worker job advertised on Craigslist.

passages.text: Knowingless is a reader-supported publication.
To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
I really needed money.
claims: The author needed money at the time.

passages.text: I was so poor I going hungry, would scrape change off the street for meals.
claims: The author was so poor that they sometimes went hungry and collected change from the street to pay for meals.

passages.text: I remember when touring a cheap room in northern Idaho to rent in a house full of strangers, they showed me the fridge, and I asked if people ever ate each other’s leftovers.
claims: While viewing an inexpensive room for rent in a shared house in northern Idaho, the author asked whether the housemates ate one another's leftovers.

passages.text: They reassured me no, of course nobody would touch your food, and I was disappointed.
claims: The people showing the author the room said that housemates would not eat one another's food, and the author felt disappointed by that answer.

passages.text: That’s not what I had been trying to ask.
claims: The author's question about leftovers was intended to ask whether they could eat food belonging to other housemates.

passages.text: I’d grown up in a very isolated, borderline-cult type of world where my parents had made it clear that they’d give me no financial assistance once I left home.
claims: The author grew up in an isolated environment and understood their parents to have said they would provide no financial assistance after the author left home.

passages.text: Once you’re 18, you’re on your own, get a job, support yourself.
claims: The author's parents told them that at age 18 they would be on their own and expected to get a job and support themselves.

passages.text: It didn’t even occur to me to let them know I was going hungry; I just figured that’s what happened to people when you were an adult.
claims: The author did not tell their parents they were going hungry because they believed going hungry was an ordinary part of being an adult.

passages.text: College wasn’t viable to me; I’d enrolled briefly but got kicked out after a few months once the finances didn’t work out.
claims: The author briefly enrolled in college but left after a few months when the finances did not work out.

passages.text: A combination of my being homeschooled my entire life (weird transcripts), my parents making just too much money for me to qualify for financial aid while simultaneously refusing to cosign any loans at all, meant my path forward was not going to be one of education.
claims: The author believed that being homeschooled, not qualifying for financial aid because of their parents' income, and having parents who would not cosign loans made pursuing further education financially impractical.

passages.text: So when Schweitzer Engineering Labs called to tell me I got the assembly line job at their Pullman manufacturing location, I was thrilled.
claims: Schweitzer Engineering Labs offered the author an assembly-line job at its Pullman manufacturing location, and the author was thrilled.

passages.text: It paid a full ten dollars an hour (in 2011).
claims: The assembly-line job at Schweitzer Engineering Labs paid the author $10 per hour in 2011.

passages.text: My last job, shelving books at the Nampa public library, had been $7.25 an hour.
claims: Before the assembly-line job, the author shelved books at the Nampa public library for $7.25 per hour.

passages.text: And the assembly line job was indoors and I didn’t have to handle any poop!
claims: The assembly-line job was indoors and did not require the author to handle feces.

passages.text: Amazing.
They said to show up at ~7am for training.
claims: The employer told the author to arrive at approximately 7 a.m. for training.

passages.text: I’d thought jobs usually started at 8am, and was disappointed that it was so early.
claims: The author had thought jobs usually began at 8 a.m. and felt disappointed that the training began earlier.

passages.text: But I was grateful to have a job at all, and I was an adult now and I knew being an adult was supposed to be very difficult, so I said ‘okay’ and showed up at 7.
claims: The author was grateful to have a job, believed adulthood was supposed to be difficult, agreed to the early start, and arrived at 7 a.m.

passages.text: They put me and other new hires in a little room and we learned about the history of the company and how electrical relays worked and how the manufacturing floor functioned and then they showed us what all the tools were, how to screw and unscrew things, how to solder, etc.
claims: During training, the author and other new hires learned about the company, electrical relays, the manufacturing floor, and how to use tools and solder.

passages.text: I liked learning things and I had a great time.
claims: The author enjoyed learning during training.

passages.text: I was determined to do awesome and I paid attention and tried super hard.
claims: The author was determined to perform well, paid attention, and worked hard during training.

passages.text: After a few days training was over, I passed their mini tests with flying colors, and they said great - show up tomorrow at 6:30am.
claims: After a few days of training, the author passed the employer's tests and was told to arrive at 6:30 a.m. the next day.

passages.text: I was oh wow.
That’s kinda early.
passages.why: The author's reaction to the start time

passages.text: They were like oh yeah right my bad, actually you’re on mandatory overtime, work starts at 5:30am.
claims: The employer told the author that the job involved mandatory overtime and that work would start at 5:30 a.m.

passages.text: I shortly find out that it’s only sometimes 5:30; much of my time working there required us clocking in before 5am.
claims: During much of the author's time at the job, workers had to clock in before 5 a.m., although the start time was sometimes 5:30 a.m.

passages.text: Oh, and you have to work Saturdays.
claims: The author was required to work Saturdays at the factory job.

passages.text: Sometimes if we’re really strapped, you need to come in on Sunday too.
claims: Workers were sometimes required to work Sundays when the factory was short-staffed or particularly busy.

passages.text: I lived 22 minutes away, so I spent my 19th year on this planet waking up at ~4:15am, getting home at 3:30pm, and going to sleep at 8pm, 6-7 days a week.
claims: While working at the factory at age 19, the author lived 22 minutes away, usually woke at about 4:15 a.m., got home at 3:30 p.m., went to sleep at 8 p.m., and followed this schedule six or seven days a week.

passages.text: I got assigned to a section near the end, where we put the relays into the metal boxes and wired then up.
claims: The author was assigned to a section near the end of the production line, where workers put relays into metal boxes and wired them.

passages.text: Everything was on the same huge floor, the units just slowly flowed down the line and got shipped out the butt end of the building.
claims: The factory's production took place on one large floor, where units moved down a line and were shipped out of the building.

passages.text: There were no windows visible to us.
claims: The author and the other workers in their area could not see any windows.

passages.text: When you arrive you get lockers where you put your stuff, and you have a little blue antistatic jacket/overcoat thing, and you put on special gloves and goggles and have to de-electrify yourself by plugging a wire from your coat into the wall.
claims: At the factory, workers stored their belongings in lockers, wore a blue antistatic overcoat, gloves, and goggles, and connected a wire from the coat to a wall outlet to discharge static electricity.

passages.text: Everything smelled SO specific, it’s hard to describe - like rubber and metal and other stuff I don’t have a term for.
claims: The author recalls that the factory had a distinctive smell, including odors they associated with rubber and metal.

passages.text: I was determined to have a good time.
claims: The author was determined to enjoy the job.

passages.text: I believed happiness was a choice, and if I just worked hard enough and was good and tried that things would go okay.
claims: At the time, the author believed that choosing happiness and working hard would make things turn out well.

passages.text: I wanted to make everyone’s lives better, so I was annoyingly cheerful.
claims: The author wanted to improve other people's lives and describes themself as excessively cheerful.

passages.text: Just downright homeschool-levels of goofy.
The units got passed down the floor on trays and these rubber pads.
claims: At the factory, units moved along the production floor on trays and rubber pads.

passages.text: When I had a little downtime (which was rare and inadvised, they told us strictly that you should be finding something to do nonstop.
claims: The author rarely had downtime at the factory, and workers were told to stay occupied continuously.

passages.text: If you are waiting for another assembler to finish their unit to pass to you, you should start immediately cleaning), I would scratch little cartoons or messages or silly things into the rubber pads.
claims: When waiting for another assembler to finish a unit, workers were expected to start cleaning; during occasional downtime, the author scratched cartoons, messages, or other marks into rubber pads.

passages.text: They were very superficial and hard to see, you had to just catch the light reflecting off of them at the right angle to notice, and if you rub it really hard it fades away.
claims: The author's marks on the rubber pads were faint, visible only at certain angles, and could be rubbed away.

passages.text: I did this for weeks.
claims: The author scratched marks into the rubber pads for weeks.

passages.text: One day I came in and my team was in a special meeting, a rare huddle.
claims: The author recalls arriving at work one day to find their team gathered for an unusual meeting.

passages.text: All the teams on the entire floor were in their own huddles.
claims: On that day, all the teams on the factory floor were gathered in separate meetings.

passages.text: They gravely told us that someone had been VANDALIZING the equipment, and that they needed to find out who it is and that terrible vandal will have to replace everything - many thousands of dollars.
claims: The author's team was told that someone had been vandalizing equipment, that the person responsible had to be identified, and that they would be required to replace equipment worth many thousands of dollars.

passages.text: I was horrified and filled with shame.
claims: The author felt horrified and ashamed after hearing the team's announcement about vandalism.

passages.text: The next day I went to a company computer and emailed someone as high up as I could find (I think possibly the CEO?) admitting it was me and I’m sorry and I don’t know how I’ll be able to pay for it but I can try somehow, maybe take it out of my wages.
claims: The day after the announcement, the author emailed a senior company employee, possibly the CEO, confessed to making the marks, apologized, and offered to try to pay for the damage, possibly through wage deductions.

passages.text: I never heard back; probably it got caught in some filter meant to prevent the plebians from reaching the consuls.
claims: The author received no response to the email and speculated that a company filter may have blocked it.

passages.text: I did this on a break.
claims: The author sent the confession email during a work break.

passages.text: We got two legally-mandated 15 minute breaks (in addition to lunch).
claims: The author says workers received two 15-minute breaks in addition to lunch, and describes those breaks as legally mandated.

passages.text: It was a big floor, and took a few minutes to walk into the break room, so the actual breaks were closer to like 9 minutes.
claims: Because it took several minutes to reach the break room, the author estimates that workers had about nine minutes of actual break time.

passages.text: The lunches were generous; we got a full 45 minutes or hour, I forget.
claims: The author's lunch break lasted either 45 minutes or an hour, though the author does not remember which.

passages.text: They gave us free lunches on Fridays, where the entire company piled into the big special lunch room and we got some kind of presentation.
claims: The company provided free lunch on Fridays, when employees gathered in a large lunch room for a presentation.

passages.text: There I got to see the other people who worked at the factory - not the assemblers, but the engineers, and the managers, and marketers, and whoever else.
claims: At the Friday lunches, the author saw factory employees such as engineers, managers, and marketers, in addition to assemblers.

passages.text: I’d watch them longingly.
claims: The author watched the factory's engineers, managers, and other non-assembly employees with longing.

passages.text: I really wanted to be one of those.
claims: The author wanted to become one of the factory's non-assembly employees.

passages.text: I had this idea that if I just worked really hard and really well on the factory floor, that eventually I could become one of them.
claims: The author believed that working hard and performing well on the factory floor might eventually lead to a non-assembly job at the company.

passages.text: I had some vague belief that I had a lot of potential.
claims: The author vaguely believed they had substantial potential.

passages.text: I was vibrating with vision and an overactive mind.
I thought I can do what they do but I have no idea how to get there.
claims: The author believed they could do the work of the factory's non-assembly employees but did not know how to reach those roles.

passages.text: Eventually I figured out this wasn’t how it worked.
claims: The author eventually concluded that working hard on the factory floor would not automatically lead to a different role at the company.

passages.text: The company advertised some educational program for assemblers to turn into brain people, but I couldn’t afford it.
claims: The company advertised an educational program intended to help assemblers move into more knowledge-based roles, but the author could not afford to participate.

passages.text: I kept meeting coworkers who’d been on the assembly line floor for decades.
claims: The author met coworkers who had worked on the assembly line for decades.

passages.text: After many months I finally get pulled into a manager’s office for a performance review and they give me a 25 cent raise.
claims: After many months at the factory, the author received a performance review and a 25-cent raise.

passages.text: I slowly lost hope.
claims: The author gradually lost hope while working at the factory.

passages.text: I really tried to hold on, but exhaustion made my fingers start slipping.
claims: The author tried to persevere, but exhaustion affected their ability to use their fingers at work.

passages.text: I was tired all the time.
claims: The author felt tired continuously while working at the factory.

passages.text: I got a friend to buy me some alcohol (19 years old remember) and started drinking many nights, which led to me being hungover and nonfunctional during the work hours.
claims: At age 19, the author had a friend buy alcohol for them, drank on many nights, and sometimes arrived at work hungover and unable to function effectively.

passages.text: I hateed the work.
claims: The author hated the factory work.

passages.text: It was a horrible no-good kind of work.
You couldn’t zone out and just do autopilot, because you had to follow a set of instructions with slight variations, that change a little each time.
claims: The factory work required workers to follow instructions that varied slightly from task to task, making it difficult to work on autopilot.

passages.text: You had to pay attention.
claims: The factory work required sustained attention.

passages.text: But the attention you paid was not interesting; it was ongoing, it was relentless, it was stupid.
My mind wasn’t mine, it was just barely pulled over some threshhold into a mind-killing, mundane amount of repetition.
I was bad at it.
claims: The author considered their performance at the factory work poor.

passages.text: Before this I’d tended to be naturally good at almost everything I tried.
claims: Before taking the factory job, the author generally found that they performed well at activities they tried.

passages.text: I learned very fast.
claims: The author describes themself as a fast learner.

passages.text: But here I made more mistakes than almost anyone else.
claims: The author believed they made more mistakes at the factory job than almost all of their coworkers.

passages.text: They tracked mistakes; people spot-checked your work, and you got an anonymized code and you could go look at a leaderboard to see where your code ranked among others.
claims: The factory tracked worker errors through spot checks and assigned workers anonymous codes that could be compared on a leaderboard.

passages.text: This depressed me more; how would I climb through the ranks and become an engineer if I accidentally screwed the blue wire onto the wrong node once every 200 times?
claims: The error rankings further discouraged the author, who worried that making an occasional wiring mistake would prevent them from becoming an engineer.

passages.text: They didn’t want us to sit, and I think I started working there at the end of some kind of sitting war, because there were a few scattered chairs and angry muttering longtimers.
claims: The author recalls that management discouraged sitting and that, when they began working there, a few chairs were available and some long-term employees expressed anger about the issue.

passages.text: Management thought sitting was bad and would destroy productivity, but some of the assemblers had fought back with cries of back pain, so they’d grudgingly allowed us a small number of chairs.
claims: Management believed sitting would reduce productivity, while some assemblers argued that standing caused back pain; the company allowed a limited number of chairs.

passages.text: I was young, so did not get first access to a chair, but I loved it when I did.
claims: The author says younger workers did not get first access to chairs and that they enjoyed sitting when they had the opportunity.

passages.text: It made my day so so much better.
claims: Sitting at work substantially improved the author's day.

passages.text: Standing hurt, and made me worse at everything, and made me tired and sad.
claims: The author says standing at work caused pain, reduced their performance, and made them tired and sad.

passages.text: After a few months I got moved up the line, to the section where they installed the boards into the units.
claims: After a few months, the author moved to a section of the production line where workers installed boards into units.

passages.text: This was less physically intensive, but more mentally draining.
claims: The author found the board-installation work less physically demanding but more mentally draining than their previous assignment.

passages.text: We assembled lots of different types of units, and the units went through different corresponding flow lines that had the required amount of tools.
claims: The factory assembled many types of units on different production lines equipped with the tools required for each line.

passages.text: But they wouldn’t let you sit and learn a single line, which might have one day allowed you to get used to it enough to zone out and have thoughts that were your own.
claims: The author says workers were not allowed to remain on one production line long enough to become thoroughly familiar with it.

passages.text: No - you had to rotate spots regularly, so that you were always just slightly unfamiliar with your current task.
claims: Workers were required to rotate positions regularly, leaving them somewhat unfamiliar with their current tasks.

passages.text: They did this so if people were out sick or something they could flexibly fill the gap, but it resulted in everyone being slightly worse at everything.
claims: The author says position rotation was intended to let workers cover for absent coworkers, but believed it made workers less proficient at each task.

passages.text: There was no groove to fall into.
It was an infinite series of tiny tasks that changed a little bit all the time, and a lot sometimes, and if you fail someone might DIE.
claims: The author describes the work as a constantly changing series of small tasks and says that an error could potentially lead to someone's death.

passages.text: And then randomly you’d get thrown into the picker role, which meant you spent the day working in the warehouse.
claims: Factory workers were sometimes assigned to a picker role in the warehouse.

passages.text: You’d have to haul in a big stacked tray on wheels and go down a list of paper and then run around the shelves pulling boxes off and scanning them and hauling the tray back.
claims: The picker role involved moving a wheeled tray, following a paper list, collecting and scanning boxes from shelves, and bringing the tray back.

passages.text: This was awesome cause it meant at least you weren’t standing still, but it was physically exhausting and happened rarely enough you never got used to it.
claims: The author enjoyed that picker work involved movement rather than standing still, but found it physically exhausting and says it happened too rarely to become familiar.

passages.text: Throughout it all, I was still grateful.
claims: The author remained grateful while working at the factory.

passages.text: I saved most of my money, and felt like a king sitting on a savings account of a few thousand dollars.
claims: The author saved most of their earnings and accumulated a savings account of a few thousand dollars.

passages.text: I was happy I was not working in poop.
claims: The author was glad their job did not involve handling feces.

passages.text: I was happy to not be hungry.
claims: The author was glad not to be hungry while working at the factory.

passages.text: But even so, the depression slowly crept around me and I had this sense that I did not want to spend the rest of my life like this.
claims: The author gradually became depressed and did not want to continue living with the same work and circumstances for the rest of their life.

passages.text: I was so confused by the coworkers that had been there for a decade+ and seemed content with their lives.
claims: The author was puzzled by coworkers who had worked at the factory for more than a decade and appeared content.

passages.text: I thought we were all on a ship that had rescued us from the void and we were so thankful and just waiting for the ship to deliver us to better lands, and so why were you still on the boat?
Why had you not gotten off?
They were all poor.
claims: The author's factory coworkers were poor.

passages.text: I had a few coworkers my age; one had come from a farm, the other wanted to do college but hadn’t managed to make it for some reason.
claims: The author had a few coworkers of a similar age; one came from a farm, and another wanted to attend college but had not managed to do so.

passages.text: Some were divorced moms, others jolly church guys.
claims: Some of the author's coworkers were divorced mothers, while others were cheerful men associated with a church.

passages.text: We all shopped at wal-mart and used coupons for groceries.
claims: The author and their coworkers shopped at Walmart and used grocery coupons.

passages.text: I wondered about their lives outside of this, but there probably wasn’t actually that much life outside of this.
claims: The author wondered about coworkers' lives outside work and speculated that they had little time for life outside the factory.

passages.text: We were with each other for the majority of our waking hours.
claims: The author and their coworkers spent most of their waking hours together at the factory.

passages.text: The factory walled us in both in space and time.
I started calling in sick more often.
claims: The author began calling in sick more frequently.

passages.text: Sometimes I’d wake up and stare at the ceiling and just completely lack the will to make myself get up and go to work.
claims: The author sometimes woke up without the will to get out of bed and go to work.

passages.text: I started bumping up against management who frowned at me for taking so many days off.
claims: The author began having conflict with managers, who disapproved of the number of days off the author took.

passages.text: My compulsive please-authority streak was not strong enough to force me out of bed, often hungover, into yet another 9-10.5 hours under flourescent lights on a Saturday.
claims: The author says their tendency to please authority figures did not overcome their reluctance to go to work, including on Saturdays when shifts lasted 9 to 10.5 hours under fluorescent lights, sometimes while hungover.

passages.text: I got out because I got another job.
claims: The author left the assembly-line job after getting another job.

passages.text: I’d been watching other job ads on craigslist and saw one opening for a boudoir photographer.
claims: Before getting the photography job, the author looked at job advertisements on Craigslist and saw an opening for a boudoir photographer.

passages.text: I liked taking photos of my pretty friends on weekends, and  so I applied, and showed them all the pretty photos I’d taken, and one day after work when I was in a hardware store they called me to tell me I was hired.
claims: The author enjoyed photographing friends on weekends, applied for the boudoir photographer opening, and showed the prospective employer photographs the author had taken.
The prospective employer called the author at a hardware store after work and told the author they had been hired.

passages.text: I almost died of joy.
I told everyone at the assembly line I was getting out, and they were so happy for me.
claims: The author told the assembly-line coworkers they were leaving, and the coworkers appeared happy for the author.

passages.text: I remember my last day clearing out my locker and walking out for the very last time and they were congratulating me and wishing me luck and then I was gone.
claims: On the author's last day at the assembly-line job, the author cleared out their locker and left, while coworkers congratulated the author and wished them luck.

passages.text: I went to the clothing store and asked the lady working there to suggest office clothes for me, because I was going to be a professional now.
claims: After leaving the assembly-line job, the author asked a clothing-store employee to recommend office clothes because the author was starting a professional job.

passages.text: She handed me a set of clothes and I bought them all.
claims: The clothing-store employee gave the author a set of clothes to consider, and the author bought all of them.

passages.text: No more blue antistatic factory coat!
The photography job lasted two weeks.
claims: The author's photography job lasted two weeks.

passages.text: I’d just turned 20 and I’d been homeschooled my whole life and I had no idea how to interact with people where I was in a role of authority.
claims: When the author started the photography job, the author had recently turned 20, had been homeschooled throughout their life, and felt unable to interact with people while in a position of authority.

passages.text: I’d had all fire quite literally beaten out of me and was compulsively submissive, quiet, nervous.
claims: The author says that they had been physically beaten and had become submissive, quiet, and nervous.

passages.text: I was not good at making strangers feel sexy and like I had everything under control in photoshoots.
claims: The author felt unable to make strangers feel attractive and confident that the author was in control during photo shoots.

passages.text: The boss called me into his office and said sorry, we need to let you go.
claims: The author's boss told the author that the employer was ending the author's employment.

passages.text: I said okay.
claims: The author responded to being fired by saying, “okay.”

passages.text: I understand.
claims: The author said they understood the decision to end their employment.

passages.text: I walked out, wearing my ill-fitting ‘office’ clothes I’d bought for this job, climbed into my beat-up little car, and wailed like death the entire drive home.
claims: After being fired, the author left wearing the office clothes bought for the job, drove home in their car, and cried throughout the drive.

passages.text: This was my one shot out into a better life and I’d blown it.
I had no idea what I was going to do, but I knew no matter what happened, I would not return to the ship that had rescued me from the void.
claims: After losing the photography job, the author did not know what to do next but was determined not to return to the assembly-line job.

passages.text: I would do anything but that.
claims: The author was determined to avoid returning to the assembly-line job.

passages.text: I had a little bit of savings to sustain me for some months, and so I began trying and failing, trying and failing, over and over again, until one day I met a man off okcupid who asked if I’d ever heard of this thing called webcamming.
claims: After losing the photography job, the author had enough savings to support them for a few months and repeatedly tried and failed to find a way forward.
The author met a man on OkCupid who asked whether the author had heard of webcamming.

passages.text: Most of the nightmares I ever have are about the factory floor.
claims: The author says that most of their nightmares involve the factory floor.

passages.text: I dream I have to go back for some reason, I’ve lost my job, I have to go recover something and they need my help and I get sucked in.
claims: The author's recurring factory-related dream involves losing a job, returning to the factory to retrieve something or help, and being drawn back into the situation.

passages.text: It’s strange for that place to be such a nightmare for me - so many other people are working there, right now as you read this, and presumably they do not feel like they’re in a nightmare.
claims: Many people work at the factory where the author used to work, and the author assumes that most of them do not experience working there as a nightmare.

passages.text: Maybe they’re good at their jobs.
claims: The author speculates that the factory's current workers may be good at their jobs.

passages.text: They get decent health insurance and plenty of money for groceries and a free lunch every Friday.
claims: The factory workers receive health insurance, enough income for groceries, and a free lunch every Friday.

passages.text: Am I weak, for failing to endure what others can thrive on?
passages.why: Rhetorical question about the author's experience

passages.text: Is something in me so brittle I had to drink to coat my exposed nerves?
I don’t know.
But I think about them a lot,
claims: The author often thinks about the factory workers.

passages.text: and I hope one day we can get a nicer, bigger boat to rescue them again.
